steps.step: Identify the variable that is null or None by reading the error message and finding the line number.
Trace back to where that variable is assigned — check if it was never initialized, or if a function returned None/null unexpectedly.
Add a null/None check before using the variable: if (obj != null) { ... } in Java/C, or if obj is not None: ... in Python.
If the variable comes from a function call (e.g., database query, file read), handle the case where it may return null by providing a default value or early return.
Consider using Optional (Java) or the walrus operator with a default (Python) to make the null case explicit and force callers to handle it.
Find the line number in the error message and identify which array, list, or string is being accessed.
Print or log the length of the array/list and the index you are trying to access just before the failing line.
Check that your loop bounds are correct — a common mistake is using <= instead of < when the upper bound is the length.
If the index is computed dynamically (e.g., from user input or an algorithm), add a bounds check: if 0 <= index < len(arr): ... .
Watch for off-by-one errors in loops: arrays are 0-indexed in most languages, so valid indices are 0 through length-1, not 1 through length.
Confirm the error is caused by infinite or excessively deep recursion by looking at the stack trace — it will show the same function repeated many times.
Check your recursive function for a missing or incorrect base case — the function must have a condition under which it returns without calling itself.
Verify that every recursive call is progressing toward the base case (e.g., the input is getting smaller each time).
If the recursion depth is genuinely large (e.g., processing a deep tree), refactor the algorithm to use an explicit stack (iterative DFS) instead of the call stack.
In Python you can inspect the current limit with sys.getrecursionlimit() and increase it with sys.setrecursionlimit(n), but this treats the symptom — fix the base case first.
Compile with debug symbols (-g flag) and run the program under a debugger (gdb or lldb) to get the exact line and variable causing the fault.
Check for null or uninitialized pointer dereference — always initialize pointers and check for NULL before dereferencing.
Check for array out-of-bounds access — ensure loop indices stay within the allocated size.
Look for use-after-free bugs — do not access a pointer after calling free() on it; set it to NULL after freeing.
Run the program with Valgrind (valgrind --leak-check=full ./program) or AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) to detect memory errors automatically.
Read the error message — it usually tells you exactly which types are involved and what operation was attempted (e.g., 'unsupported operand type(s) for +: int and str').
Use print(type(variable)) in Python or check types with instanceof / typeof in Java/JavaScript to confirm the actual runtime type of the variable.
Check if the variable comes from external input (user input, file, API) — such data is often a string that needs to be converted: int(value), float(value), etc.
Look for implicit type coercion in mixed-type expressions — in Python 3, dividing two integers with / gives a float; use // for integer division.
Add explicit type annotations (Python type hints, Java generics) to catch type mismatches earlier during development.
Read the error message — the line number and a caret (^) usually point to the exact location of the syntax error.
Check the line indicated AND the line immediately before it — syntax errors often result from a missing closing bracket, parenthesis, or colon on the previous line.
Verify that all opening brackets, parentheses, and braces have a matching closing character — use your editor's bracket matching feature.
In Python, check for mixed tabs and spaces in indentation — use only spaces (4 per level) or only tabs, never both.
Copy the error into a search engine — syntax errors have distinctive messages that are well-documented with examples and fixes.
Confirm the exact module name in the error message and check your import statement for typos — module names are case-sensitive.
Verify the package is installed: run pip show <package-name> (Python) or npm list <package> (Node.js); if it is not installed, run pip install <package> or npm install <package>.
Check that you are running your code in the correct virtual environment — the package may be installed in a different environment.
If you are importing your own module, confirm the file exists at the expected path relative to the script and that the directory contains an __init__.py (for Python packages).
Check sys.path in Python (import sys; print(sys.path)) to see the directories Python searches for modules — add the correct path if needed.
Find the variable name in the error message and search for where it is (or should be) defined in your code.
Check for typos in the variable name — 'username' and 'userName' are different variables in most languages.
Verify the variable is defined before it is used — in Python, execution is sequential, so using a variable before its assignment raises NameError.
Check variable scope — a variable defined inside a function (local scope) is not accessible outside it; if you need it outside, return it or define it at the broader scope.
In JavaScript, check whether you used var, let, or const — var has function scope while let/const have block scope; using a variable outside its block raises ReferenceError.
Interrupt the program (Ctrl+C or kill the process) and add print statements inside the loop to trace the loop variable and termination condition on each iteration.
Check that the loop's termination condition can actually become true — for example, a while loop where the counter is never incremented will run forever.
Verify that variables modified inside the loop are the same ones checked in the condition — a common bug is modifying a copy rather than the original.
For recursive algorithms, check that the recursive call reduces the problem toward the base case — a non-reducing call leads to infinite recursion.
Consider adding a safety counter (iteration_limit = 10000; if count > iteration_limit: break) during debugging to prevent the program from hanging.
Trace the loop manually with a small example (e.g., array of 3 elements) and verify the first and last iterations hit the correct indices.
Check whether your loop condition uses < or <= — for a zero-indexed array of length n, the correct condition is i < n, not i <= n (which would access index n, out of bounds).
When iterating a range that represents a count (e.g., 'do this 5 times'), use range(5) in Python or i=0; i<5 in C/Java, which gives indices 0,1,2,3,4.
When computing mid in binary search or divide-and-conquer, prefer mid = low + (high - low) // 2 to avoid overflow and ensure consistent rounding.
Add an assertion after the loop that checks the final state (e.g., assert result_count == expected_count) to catch off-by-one errors automatically during testing.
Profile memory usage with a tool: Valgrind for C/C++, memory_profiler or tracemalloc for Python, VisualVM for Java. Identify which objects are growing without bound.
Look for long-lived data structures (global lists, caches, event listener registries) that accumulate references without removing old ones.
In C/C++, ensure every malloc/new is paired with a free/delete, especially on error paths. Use smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) to automate this.
In Python, check for reference cycles or lingering references in closures, class attributes, or global variables. Use gc.collect() and gc.get_objects() to inspect.
In Java/Python, remove event listeners, close file handles and database connections, and clear caches with a size limit (e.g., LRU cache) to prevent unbounded growth.
Find the division operation in the error's line number and identify the divisor variable.
Add a guard condition before the division: if denominator != 0: result = numerator / denominator else: handle_zero_case().
Trace back to where the divisor is set — check if it can be zero due to a calculation result, empty list length, or uninitialized value.
If the denominator is user-supplied or computed from data, validate it with an assert or raise a descriptive ValueError before the division.
For floating-point code, also guard against very small values (near-zero) that can cause numerical instability even if not exactly zero.

default_steps.step: Read the full error message carefully — it usually states the error type, the file name, and the line number where the error occurred.
Navigate to the indicated line number in your editor and read the surrounding 5-10 lines for context.
Add print/log statements around the failing code to trace the values of variables just before the error occurs.
Search for the exact error message (in quotes) in a search engine — most common errors have well-known solutions documented on Stack Overflow and official documentation.
Reproduce the error with a minimal example — strip your code down to the smallest program that still triggers the bug. This often reveals the root cause and makes it easier to ask for help.
